recentItems.title: COP31: How wild weather swept around the globe in 2026
recentItems.description:
2026 has been another year of wild weather, with tropical cyclone, fire tornadoes and wildfires. 62% of cumulative human-caused CO₂ emissions between 1850 and 2019 occurred during 1970–2019—a 50-year period, according to the IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change). Those emissions create heat, which scrambles weather patterns and ecosystems.

recentItems.title: Funerals for police and civilians killed in Russian attack on Ukraine's Komyshuvakha
recentItems.description:
Police officers and relatives gathered in Zaporizhzhia for a farewell ceremony for six police officers killed in Russian attacks in the frontline village of Komyshuvakha. The attack killed at least 55 civilians, while 45 more people remain missing, according to local authorities. (AP Video by Vasilisa Stepanenko / Production by Volodymyr Yurchuk)

recentItems.title: COP31: A look back at how ice is retreating across the globe
recentItems.description:
Vast shrinkage of glaciers in Greenland and Antarctica over the last half-century or so has caused the loss of 11 trillion tons of ice, according to data from the European Space Agency (ESA), raising global sea levels by more than three centimeters. Ahead of the COP31 in Turkey this month, the State of the Cryosphere report says that missing the 1.5°C Paris Agreement target "will bring large-scale, and in many cases irreversible, impacts from the Earth’s melting ice sheets, permafrost, glaciers, sea ice and polar oceans."

recentItems.title: COP31 explained: Why the UN climate summit matters
recentItems.description:
World leaders are preparing to join tens of thousands of delegates in Turkey for the COP31 climate summit. They are set to discuss the progress countries have made towards meeting their climate goals, including reducing greenhouse gas emissions. But what exactly is COP and is it helping to tackle climate change?

recentItems.title: COP31: How drought and heat have impacted lives across the globe in 2026
recentItems.description:
2026 was an exceptionally hot summer for many in the Northern Hemisphere and it looks like there is more to come. If all the countries do what they promise to reduce heat-trapping emissions, Earth will likely still warm another 2.2 degrees Fahrenheit (1.2 degrees Celsius) above current temperatures, according to a recent update of climate calculations by the United Nations Environment Programme. That’s about two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit (0.1 degrees Celsius) more than last year’s projections by the same science team.
(Video produced by: Siobhan Starrs)
